title: Quiet Loop
user: Adult language learners who want a sustainable 10-minute review habit without streaks, feeds, or punitive notifications.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo language-app maker asks whether deliberately avoiding gamification, streaks, subscriptions, and engagement tricks is commercially viable; the thread contains 67 comments.
A reviewer asks for an Archive action because a card can stop being useful while the source note remains valuable.

recurrence: Two separate 2025–26 learning-tool communities identify the same retention risk: engagement mechanics and endless review queues make a tool less useful, not more. The HN discussion is substantial (67 comments).
current_workaround: Use Duolingo/Anki despite unwanted mechanics, turn off notifications, or abandon stale cards manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Duolingo optimizes habit loops and Anki optimizes scheduling; neither makes a calm, finite daily routine with first-class card retirement its main product promise.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first PWA with one bounded daily set, optional weekly planning, a one-tap archive-with-reason action, and exportable CSV. Non-goals: a language course, social feed, generated lessons, or streaks.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 50% of activated users complete at least 12 sessions without enabling a streak or push notification, and 30% archive or revise an obsolete item.
monetization: one-time — the audience explicitly values an unpressured, subscription-free learning environment.
constraints: Store learning data on device by default; provide export/delete; do not imply pedagogical outcomes; accessibility must include keyboard-only review.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately finite review ritual and content-retirement tool, rather than another gamified language app or an Anki clone.

title: Context Cloze
user: Vocabulary learners and teachers who need learners to retrieve a word from a meaningful sentence rather than recognize a card face.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a vocabulary-methods thread, a commenter explicitly rejects flashcards in favor of open fill-in-the-blank questions because they prevent rote learning.
A user reports that sentence-ending question marks in card content are misread as card syntax and truncate the editor view, showing brittle authoring around real sentence material.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 reports: learners want sentence-level recall, while authors encounter card tooling that treats normal prose as fragile markup.
current_workaround: Hand-write blanks in Google Docs, use a general quiz maker, or force sentences into flashcard syntax.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki and Quizlet support cloze-like cards, but their authoring is card-first and syntax-heavy; generic quiz products do not keep a small reusable personal sentence bank.
smallest_useful_product: A browser tool to paste a sentence, mark one or two blanks, attach a definition/note, and run typed-answer practice with printable and CSV export. Non-goals: auto-generating vocabulary, grading essays, or hosting public decks.
success_measure: At least 40% of pilot authors create 20 sentence prompts and learners answer 70% of them in a second session seven days later.
monetization: free — a portable, no-login sentence-practice utility needs easy classroom and self-learner adoption.
constraints: No copyrighted corpus bundled; users provide sentences; support Unicode/RTL and keyboard input; do not collect student text.
why_distinct: The unit is an editable, context-rich typed retrieval prompt, not a generic flashcard or an LLM quiz generator.

title: Glyph Bridge
user: Learners of Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, and other script-heavy languages who need to see writing, pronunciation, and meaning together during recall.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A vocabulary-retention asker specifically asks whether learner-controlled words, sentences, context, and audio would improve long-term recall.
A feature request asks for a third always-visible field on bidirectional cards specifically for glyphic/logographic language study.

recurrence: Two recent, independent requests converge on the missing three-way bridge between form, reading, and meaning; it is a high-frequency pain for every new word in script-heavy languages.
current_workaround: Overload an Anki card template, put pronunciation in a hint field, or maintain separate character and vocabulary decks.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki templates are powerful but technical; Duolingo and Memrise own their content. Neither offers a simple personal three-field recall flow with reading hidden or revealed deliberately.
smallest_useful_product: An offline deck builder with glyph, pronunciation, meaning, example sentence, and optional user-recorded audio; practice modes hide exactly one layer at a time. Non-goals: an entire language curriculum, OCR, or public deck marketplace.
success_measure: 60% of pilot users create 50+ entries and use at least two reveal modes within 21 days.
monetization: one-time — a focused personal-study tool should not meter cards or audio recordings.
constraints: Unicode, CJK fonts, ruby text, RTL, and offline media storage are core; only user-provided audio/content; export must be interoperable.
why_distinct: It is designed around three-layer script recall rather than adding another two-sided card template to a general SRS.

title: Repair Queue
user: Self-learners with established decks who need to find badly phrased, ambiguous, or persistently forgotten prompts without judging their own recall quality every time.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner asks why flashcard apps require a self-rated Good/Average/Bad judgment instead of measuring how memorization is going.
An Anki user requests a proportional forgotten-rate search because raw lapse counts obscure which cards are genuinely problematic.

recurrence: Two recent reports from different communities ask for better diagnosis of memory quality than subjective grades or absolute lapse counts.
current_workaround: Self-rate every card, search absolute lapses, or periodically browse a deck by hand.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki exposes reviews, lapses, and FSRS statistics, but does not provide a lightweight repair workflow that turns error patterns into revise/split/archive decisions.
smallest_useful_product: A local importer for Anki CSV/review exports that ranks items by recent failure ratio and response time, then offers revise, split, suspend, and archive checklists. Non-goals: replacing Anki scheduling, cloud sync, or claiming cognitive diagnosis.
success_measure: Pilot users repair 15 flagged cards and reduce their flagged-card failure rate by 20% after four weeks.
monetization: one-time — analysis runs locally on an existing study history and has no recurring service cost.
constraints: All deck history stays local; make scoring explainable; no health or learning-disability claims; preserve original exports.
why_distinct: It improves the quality of the learner's prompts rather than competing as another review scheduler.

title: Source Study Map
user: Professionals and advanced students learning a new domain who need to turn scattered source notes into a compact, reviewable map of concepts, examples, and unresolved questions.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An asker says retaining domain knowledge is as hard as technical knowledge and asks how people capture, transfer, and study shared mental models.
A flashcard user reports substantially different open-card counts across devices after sync, highlighting the fragility of relying on a note/SRS system as the sole knowledge store.

recurrence: One 2025 learning-system request and one 2025 reliability report point to a repeatable need: keep a source-linked mental model separate from the reviewer implementation.
current_workaround: Mix notes, bookmarks, diagrams, and flashcards in one app, then hope sync and links stay coherent.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, Obsidian, Logseq, and Anki each cover pieces; none makes a small portable map of claim → source → example → self-test the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app that stores a concept graph with source URLs, one concrete example, one question, and Markdown/CSV export. Non-goals: collaborative wiki, general note-taking replacement, AI summarization, or sync service.
success_measure: At least half of pilot users create a 25-node map and reopen a source from the map during a practical task within 30 days.
monetization: one-time — personal professional learning data benefits from a durable local file format.
constraints: Keep URLs and user notes local; provide plain-text export; no scraping/paywalled-content ingestion; accessible graph view needs list equivalent.
why_distinct: It structures verifiable learning relationships, not an undifferentiated personal knowledge base or card deck.

title: Concept Card Workshop
user: Instructors teaching procedural or safety concepts who need a fast way to run a small-group, discussion-led card exercise after a lecture.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner describes a difficult avalanche-risk lecture becoming understandable when the instructor switched to physical Snow Safety Cards, and asks about games/cards for learning skills.
A parent reports that a daughter who uses flashcards heavily encountered a serious scheduling-algorithm failure, reinforcing the value of activities that do not depend on a black-box review queue.

recurrence: The 2026 firsthand classroom-to-cards account and 2025 heavy-user reliability issue both favor transparent, instructor-led practice over a fragile individual SRS loop.
current_workaround: Buy specialized card decks, improvise slips of paper, or lecture again with discussion questions.
incumbents_and_gap: Quizlet Live and Kahoot are screen-centric competition products; commercial training decks are domain-specific. Teachers lack a neutral printable builder for scenario, evidence, decision, and consequence cards.
smallest_useful_product: A static-web card-set composer with four card roles, printable cut sheets, a facilitator timer, and a no-account join code for optional projection. Non-goals: graded assessments, public marketplaces, generated lesson content, or student profiling.
success_measure: Ten pilot facilitators each run one 15-minute activity; at least 70% report every group contributed one defensible decision in the debrief.
monetization: freemium — free single-set printing invites teacher adoption; paid offline pack templates can support niche professional training.
constraints: No bundled regulated/safety curriculum; teacher owns content and outcomes; printable PDFs need accessible text alternatives and browser-only generation.
why_distinct: It creates facilitated reasoning games from teacher-authored material, not another solitary flashcard or points quiz.

title: Human Computer Stations
user: Elementary teachers introducing algorithms to 8–11-year-olds who need a low-prep, device-light activity that makes precision, sequencing, roles, and conditions tangible.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A classroom volunteer asks for a second-generation software-development introduction for 3rd–5th graders after a literal PB&J algorithm exercise worked, and commenters propose roles and distributed instructions.

Kolibri tracks a product issue where a gap-match assessment interaction fails for learners, evidence that even established learning platforms have trouble delivering basic interactive practice reliably.

recurrence: A detailed teacher request plus a current assessment-interaction failure show that hands-on, printable teaching has a robust role alongside classroom software.
current_workaround: Invent a PB&J demo, write role cards by hand, use Blockly/Code.org, or depend on a classroom app working that day.
incumbents_and_gap: Scratch and Code.org teach on screens; unplugged-CS lesson sites are often static PDFs. The gap is a reusable station generator with roles, hidden constraints, and differentiated difficulty.
smallest_useful_product: A static generator for printable four-station packs: instruction writer, executor, debugger, and tester; includes sequencing/loop/conditional variants and teacher debrief prompts. Non-goals: coding curriculum, student accounts, analytics, or collecting child data.
success_measure: Eight teachers run a pack with 20+ pupils; 75% say students can explain one ambiguity or condition discovered during the activity.
monetization: free — broad teacher reuse and trust matter more than extracting payment for a small classroom utility.
constraints: COPPA/child privacy: no accounts or telemetry; provide print accessibility, harmless materials guidance, and teacher-controlled content.
why_distinct: It is an adaptive, printable orchestration tool for an unplugged lesson, not a junior coding app.

title: Lesson Packet
user: Teachers who want to distribute a small activity, reflection, and exit check as one durable offline file without accounts, subscriptions, or data collection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A teacher says they built teaching and productivity tools as single HTML files because they were tired of subscriptions and paywalls; the post emphasizes no server, login, or API calls.
A current Kolibri coach report says learner-progress values do not update automatically in a course table, exposing a cost of depending on centralized progress dashboards for a small activity.

recurrence: A teacher-led 2025 call for downloadable tools and a 2026 classroom-platform progress defect both support lightweight artifacts that still work when backend state is stale or unavailable.
current_workaround: Use Google Forms/Classroom, photocopy worksheets, or hand-build ad hoc HTML files.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Classroom, Canvas, and Kolibri manage whole courses; worksheet editors produce paper. They do not make a one-file, interactive lesson packet with optional local student save and teacher-readable export easy.
smallest_useful_product: A browser composer that produces one self-contained HTML packet with instructions, sortable/checkable activity blocks, a reflection box, and a download-only response file. Non-goals: LMS integration, remote grading, accounts, analytics, or AI lesson generation.
success_measure: At least 20 teachers export a packet and 50% report using it with a class or tutoring group within 45 days.
monetization: free — offline portability is central to the problem and avoids a recurring infrastructure burden.
constraints: No student data leaves the device; sanitize imported templates; support printing and low-end browsers; teacher must supply licensed content.
why_distinct: It packages a small interactive lesson as a file, sitting between a worksheet and a full LMS.

title: Practice Evidence Log
user: Working professionals who study 30–60 minutes around a job and need to connect deliberate practice to the real troubleshooting situations it improves.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A root-cause analyst studies dense software material and makes flashcards because constant lookup limits diagnosis, while explicitly trying to protect work-life balance with 30–60 minute sessions.
A report says Anki's Desired Retention simulator crashes for a default-FSRS deck, leaving a learner unable to use its promised study-time/retention trade-off aid.

recurrence: The 2025 professional-learning account and 2026 retention-planning defect both show a need for grounded evidence of what limited study time actually helps with.
current_workaround: Track time in a todo app, make flashcards, and rely on a vague sense that study helped at work.
incumbents_and_gap: Anki estimates review scheduling and time trackers log minutes; neither links a practice session to a later real-world application or an unanswered question.
smallest_useful_product: A local weekly log with topic, 10–60 minute practice block, source, one retrieval prompt, and a later 'used in work' note; it shows evidence without gamified totals. Non-goals: employee surveillance, team performance reporting, content generation, or replacing SRS.
success_measure: 40% of pilot users record three application links in their first month and report one reduced lookup loop or faster diagnosis.
monetization: one-time — private professional learning records should remain portable and not invite employer data collection.
constraints: Default local storage and export; warn users not to paste confidential employer data; no productivity or performance claims.
why_distinct: It measures transfer from practice to application, rather than maximizing study minutes or card reviews.

title: Subtitle Ladder
user: Independent spoken-language learners who want repeatable listening-and-speaking practice that gradually removes translation support.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A learner seeking conversational German receives advice to use comprehensible input and a step-down sequence from target-audio/English subtitles to target subtitles to no subtitles.
AnkiDroid's current custom-study-by-tags UX work demonstrates that learners need narrower study subsets rather than one undifferentiated review queue.

recurrence: A direct 2025 spoken-language request and a 2025 study-subset UX issue both point to the need to control difficulty and scope deliberately.
current_workaround: Rewatch videos while manually changing subtitle settings, save timestamps in notes, or make separate decks by difficulty.
incumbents_and_gap: Language Reactor and streaming subtitles help consume media; Anki schedules words. Neither is a local, repeatable ladder for a learner's own short licensed/public-domain clips and recordings.
smallest_useful_product: A PWA that accepts user-recorded or public-domain audio plus a caption file, creates 15–60 second loops, and offers translation, target-text, masked-word, and no-text stages with a spoken self-recording. Non-goals: downloading commercial video, machine translation, speech scoring, or content catalog.
success_measure: Half of pilots complete the same clip in three support levels and make at least five self-recordings in two weeks.
monetization: one-time — local media practice has no ongoing serving cost and avoids copyrighted-content dependence.
constraints: Only user-owned, licensed, or public-domain media; keep recordings local; captions require Unicode/RTL support; no fluency claims.
why_distinct: It operationalizes a gradual support-removal practice routine rather than providing another course or subtitle browser extension.

title: Audio Margin
user: Students and professionals attending Spanish-language classes or meetings who need private, time-linked notes and recall prompts from recordings.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user explicitly asks for a Fathom/Granola-like note-taking app that transcribes Spanish.
AnkiDroid users report that large numeric progress dialogs make progress hard to estimate quickly, a reminder that study-session feedback must be legible rather than merely voluminous.

recurrence: The direct 2026 Spanish-transcription request and 2025 study UX report show a narrow need for language-appropriate capture plus legible, bounded follow-up.
current_workaround: Use English-first meeting transcription products, take separate notes, or transcribe manually before making review cards.
incumbents_and_gap: Fathom, Granola, Otter, and Notta are meeting systems; Anki is a reviewer. The gap is a private study margin that turns timestamps into a few learner-authored recall cues without becoming a meeting archive.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop-local app that runs a selectable on-device Spanish speech model, shows a time-linked transcript, and lets users pin a sentence with their own note/question; session view caps the next review at five pins. Non-goals: cloud meeting bot, speaker surveillance, automatic flashcard generation, or hosted recordings.
success_measure: In pilot use, 60% of sessions produce 3–8 pinned prompts and users revisit at least one pin within seven days.
monetization: one-time — local transcription and sensitive audio make an offline license more credible than a recurring cloud plan.
constraints: Obtain consent before recording; process audio locally; model licenses must permit redistribution; support deletion and Spanish regional variants.
why_distinct: It is a learner-owned margin around audio, with deliberate small recall follow-up, not an AI meeting-summary wrapper.

title: Syllabus Practice Box
user: Teachers and parents with licensed or self-authored high-school materials who need offline, syllabus-bounded practice on low-connectivity devices.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An asker wants a tiny, fully offline mobile assistant for three high-school subjects using a syllabus, textbooks, practice questions, past papers, and answers.
A coach reports confusing Progress versus Learner progress values when a pre-test has not started, demonstrating that offline-learning progress needs clear, activity-level semantics.

recurrence: A 2025 request for offline high-school practice and a 2026 offline-learning-platform progress problem both surface the same need: reliable local materials and transparent progress, not a generic chatbot.
current_workaround: Use paper past papers, a full Kolibri deployment, or attempt to build an on-device RAG tutor.
incumbents_and_gap: Kolibri is a broad offline learning platform and Khanmigo/ChatGPT are cloud assistants. There is room for a small, teacher-owned practice player that is explicitly restricted to vetted questions and answer explanations.
smallest_useful_product: An Android offline package player that imports a teacher-authored topic manifest, questions, worked answers, and lightweight attachments; it reports completed/attempted/not-yet-started per topic. Non-goals: LLM chat, auto-generated exam questions, textbook bundling, remote proctoring, or a learning-management system.
success_measure: Three pilot educators package one subject each; 70% of learner sessions complete a topic with an unambiguous completion state while offline.
monetization: free — offline access and teacher-controlled materials are the core value; paid authoring support can be evaluated only after usage.
constraints: Import only materials the educator has rights to distribute; encrypt optional local student records; accessibility and low-storage support are essential; do not market it as an exam guarantee.
why_distinct: It removes the speculative tutor model and focuses on trustworthy, offline execution of an educator's existing practice set.
